Busy with Waz and Da‘wah: How Much Do We Practise What We Preach in Our Professional Responsibilities?

A recurring criticism is often heard regarding our respected *wa‘iz* (Islamic preachers). Many of them serve as lecturers, Hadith teachers, or in other positions at various madrasas. Yet, particularly during the preaching season, they are frequently seen rushing from one religious gathering to another, sometimes within nearby areas and sometimes travelling long distances.

Their dedication and commitment to spreading the message of Islam are undoubtedly important. However, alongside this, an equally relevant professional question inevitably arises: how do they balance these extensive commitments of time and effort with their institutional teaching responsibilities?

When a teacher regularly participates in one gathering, meeting, or event after another, it is natural to ask: Is he able to conduct his scheduled classes on time? Are his academic responsibilities towards his students being fulfilled properly? Or does his involvement in *da‘wah* activities sometimes result in unavoidable shortcomings in his institutional duties?

The question does not end there. If a teacher regularly receives a salary and benefits from an employer without properly fulfilling the responsibilities agreed upon, the matter is no longer merely one of administrative or professional discipline; it also becomes a question of professional ethics and the fulfilment of a trust (*amanah*).

Of course, I am not qualified to issue a definitive Shariah ruling on whether someone’s salary or benefits are *halal* or *haram*, nor am I a *mufti*. Nevertheless, there can be little doubt that the ethical and Shariah-related implications of receiving remuneration while neglecting one’s responsibilities deserve serious consideration.

This issue also brings my own position to mind.

I, too, am a humble teacher. From time to time, I receive invitations from regional, national, and even international sources to participate in seminars, conferences, discussions, and various other events.

However, because I must balance these invitations with my university responsibilities, scheduled classes, examinations, and academic and administrative duties, I am unable to accept most of them. In fact, I get the opportunity to attend only a very small number of such events.

Even so, I sometimes ask myself whether I am fulfilling my own professional responsibilities with sufficient dedication.

Yesterday, a ceremony was scheduled at the Baitul Mukarram Islamic Book Fair in Dhaka to unveil the cover of one of my new books. Several distinguished scholars and *ulama* from the country were expected to attend.

Today, I was also invited to a reception at the Sheraton in Dhaka, organised by the Saudi Embassy to mark Saudi Arabia’s 96th National Day.

Personally, I was interested in attending both events. However, because of departmental commitments and examination-related responsibilities, I was unable to attend either.

There is no reason to interpret this as self-praise. Rather, it is simply an ordinary reflection of professional accountability.

When a teacher joins an institution, a specific portion of his time and effort is entrusted to that institution and its students. Therefore, no matter how prestigious, attractive, or socially significant an external commitment may be, it should not be allowed to overshadow his primary responsibilities. This is a principle that one must remember, at the very least, in one’s own professional life.

However, this question does not apply only to *wa‘iz* or madrasa teachers. There are also many teachers in other educational institutions, including universities, who give greater priority to external engagements, social commitments, business, organisational activities, events, or personal pursuits than to their core teaching responsibilities.

As a result, problems such as irregular attendance in the classroom, insufficient time devoted to students, and negligence in assessment and other academic duties can sometimes arise. Teaching then appears to become less of a primary profession and more of an institutional affiliation that serves as a professional identity alongside numerous other activities.

The issue is even more sensitive in the case of a *da‘i* or Islamic preacher.

The reason is simple: a preacher does not merely deliver speeches. He teaches people about principles, morality, trustworthiness, responsibility, and integrity. The influence of his message is not confined to the words he utters from the pulpit; his personal and professional conduct also becomes a form of silent *da‘wah*.

Therefore, someone who teaches others to be responsible is expected to demonstrate the same sense of responsibility in his own conduct. Someone who speaks about trustworthiness should be equally careful to honour the professional trust placed in him. And someone who teaches others the value of time should ensure that the time allocated to his own responsibilities is not devalued in favour of other commitments.

Ultimately, the issue is not whether one should participate in religious gatherings or refrain from doing so. Nor is it a matter of creating an artificial conflict between *da‘wah* and teaching. The real question concerns the proper prioritisation and balancing of entrusted responsibilities.

A person may simultaneously be a teacher, a *da‘i*, an author, a speaker, or an organiser. However, none of these roles should ever become an excuse for neglecting another responsibility that has been entrusted to him.

In particular, those who teach others about ideals and morality should be able to answer one question clearly in their own lives:

**How much of the morality and sense of responsibility that we preach do we actually practise in our own conduct and professional lives?**
